sections.overview: Archips oporana is a tortricid moth known as the Pine Tortrix. It is native in Belgium, where it is fairly common in the north and much rarer in the south.
sections.identification: The male spans 19–21 mm; the larger female spans 22–28 mm. Males have purple-brown forewings and dark grey-brown hindwings, while females show chestnut markings and a fine, net-like wing pattern. It resembles the related Archips podana and Archips betulana; the male's darker hindwings and the female's wing pattern help separate it from those lookalikes.
sections.habitat: It occurs in conifer woodland and plantations; in parts of south-east England it is scarce and has recently been recorded at only a few sites.
sections.diet: The larvae feed on conifers such as Scots pine, silver fir, Norway spruce and juniper.
sections.behavior: Adults are active from afternoon or dusk and may come to lights later in the evening. In some regions they fly from late May into July, with a partial later generation reported in Belgium.
sections.reproduction: Caterpillars appear in autumn, overwinter among bound needles, and resume feeding on fresh shoots in spring; pupation takes place at the feeding site in early summer. Accounts differ by region: one German guide describes one annual generation, while the Belgian catalogue reports two, with only a partial second brood.
sections.ecology: By feeding within conifer needles and young shoots, larvae can damage new growth; attacked shoot axes may die, bend or break.
sections.conservation: The Hampshire source calls it nationally scarce in south-east England; this is a regional category and not a global assessment.
